utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Is the Gotovina Defence ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as far as I understand, there will be no application for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's correct. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness, which will be Mr. Bilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, it's Veselko Bilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we will be moving pursuant to 92 ter with this witness statement. I neglected, Mr. President, to advise the witness of the witness summary. I just wanted to advise you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will briefly explain to him what the purpose is. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think the motion was filed last night, and we have no objections to this witness being 92 ter'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's already on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bilic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher, and I would like to invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Bilic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we start, I have remembered certain details in the mean time, and I just wanted to let the Honourable Chamber know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you want to give further details. You can do so during the examination. And you will first be examined by Mr. Kehoe, and he will certainly give you an opportunity to give further details which you have apparently not yet raised with the Gotovina Defence. Please be seated. Don't worry, an opportunity will you given to you. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I understand in talking to Mr. Misetic in hearing the Croatian said that he has some notes that he would like to use during the course of his testimony to refer to. So maybe there was some lack of clarity as to what he was saying and what question Your Honour answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to find out. Did you want to address the Chamber because you wanted to give further details; or did you intend to say that you had written down some details which you might like to consult when examined. Could you explain which of the two it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I merely remembered certain details, since I knew I was about to start giving my testimony. The information isn't that important, although it is important for me. But it relates to the start of all these events in 1991. It may not be that important to you, in view of my actions following Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest to you that you'll first answer any questions put to you by Mr. Kehoe. It may well be that some matters will be dealt with. If not, you'll have an opportunity. But I do agree with you that the focus of this case is not what happened in 1991, although not irrelevant, but we'll then see. You'll first now be examined by Mr. Kehoe, who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, can you state your name for the record and spell your last name, sir.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: My name is Veselko Bilic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness be asked to approach the microphones, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: My name is Veselko Bilic, aka Srecko. I was born in 1957 in the village of Krkovici. I currently reside in Knin. Simunoviceva Street, number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, some preliminary questions, do you recall meeting members of the Gotovina Defence team on the 18th of June, 2009, a little bit more than a week ago?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you recall signing a statement that day?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could bring up on the screen 65 ter 1D2767.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The document that's on the screen, Mr. Bilic, do you recognise that as the document that you signed on the 18th of June, 2009?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to review that document before you came in to court today?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bilic, let me take you -- not yesterday but the day before, two days ago, on 29th of June, did you have a chance to meet with members of the Gotovina Defence team here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did you provide certain clarifications to your statement during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2 of this document and focussing on paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did you tell the Gotovina Defence at the time of Operation Storm that you were not formally mobilised before Storm, but, rather, you went to the meeting point on your own initiative? Did you tell them that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it's an important issue, these issues about mobilisation and demobilisation, and I would suggest to ask in non-leading format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, I'm just --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... it's a matter that can be refreshed, but the first attempt should be made to elicit from the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, what we have is a 92 ter statement. We usually move to have that tendered so that we have a basis for the evidence. We have a supplemental information sheet, which arrived rather late, as a matter of fact. If there's anything in that supplemental information sheet then, of course, it could go the same course. But if there is anything outside of these documents, then I would agree with Mr. Waespi that questions should be put in a non-leading way, if there's objection against leading. But since you were talking about the 29th of June conversations, I'm just going through it, whether I ... Yes, I think, Mr. Waespi, we find it in the first paragraph of the supplemental information sheet. Now, if the witness would have read that and would have attested to its truthfulness, then the whole issue of leading would not exist anymore. Apart from that, if it has been part of a conversation which was held the day before yesterday with the witness, then, of course, but that might in more general terms be true, that the whole rule on leading, if the parties had ample opportunities to proof witnesses and to, of course -- becomes a bit, well, relative, to say the least. Under those circumstances and finding in the supplemental information sheet which I take it could be dealt with in such a way, do you still insist on a non-leading way of putting to the witness any matter which is in the supplemental information sheet?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I leave it into your hands, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I will be mindful of counsel's concerns to try to limit that as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, did you tell the Gotovina Defence that you were not formally mobilised prior to Operation Storm but you went to the meeting point on your own initiative?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I stated that. I was demobilised in 1995, some time before Operation Storm. I don't know exactly the date, but I presume it can be found in the records. Already in 1994 I was invalided from the war because I had been wounded in 1992, in fact. I got 60 per cent invalidity. I was not feeling well, and I was thinking about going into retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think you answered the question for us. If we could just move -- Mr. Bilic, if you could just move a bit towards the microphone for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it's an issue of his chair. I think it is difficult to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it could be that an adjustment of the chair might -- if you sit more upright and perhaps the -- these chairs are a bit --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think if we lock it, Mr. President, so it doesn't go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm also struggling with these chairs, Mr. Bilic, so ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm heavy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not the difference, Mr. Bilic. Is that better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, when you went to this meeting point, did you receive a weapon?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you turn that weapon back in?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What date did you turn it back in?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 1 of your statement you say: "I was a member of the 15th Home Guards Brigade until the 18th of August, 1995." Is that what you're corresponding to with the date that you turned your weapon in?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday did you have another meeting with the Gotovina Defence where you discussed some other matters in your statement?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't remember what it was that I said. I may have remembered some additional details that are not that significant. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, what we're trying to do is we're trying to get your witness statement as accurate as possible for the Chamber. And let me assist you in this regard. In paragraph 4 of your statement where you're talking about the villages that you went through, you noted --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, this is approximately halfway down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted that you entered into the village of Lazanice. And did you tell that -- the Gotovina Defence team that you weren't sure if it was Lazanice or Travice?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I remember that. I couldn't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with -- other than these clarifications, Mr. Bilic, is the statement that's on the screen -- is that statement -- does that accurately reflect what you told the Gotovina Defence team on the 18th of June, 2009?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And is this information that you provide in the statement, is that true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. 100 per cent. I only said that I couldn't remember the date when we got into Kistanje, whether it was the 6th or the 7th, but for the rest, that's true. I don't have anything else to add to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Save for the fact that we were too lenient because our commanders halted us in our advancement. We could have achieved what we achieved sooner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, sir, and we can -- we'll get to some of those subjects in a bit. I'm just trying to cover some preliminaries with regard to the statement. Now, once again staying with the statement, Mr. Bilic, if I asked you the same questions regarding the matters that were discussed in the statement, would your answers be the same today as those that you gave in that statement?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, well offer into evidence 65 1D2767.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1547.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. The supplemental information sheet will be tendered, will not be tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It had not been translated, Mr. President, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has not been translated. So therefore the witness has had no opportunity to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then this would be the moment, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, the public is following these proceedings, and since your statement is admitted into evidence, the public would not know what is approximately in your statement. Therefore, a summary will be read by Mr. Kehoe. You don't have to answer. It just summarizes what is in your statement so that the public knows and is able to follow when we continue. Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Bilic testified that he and his family were refugees from Krkovic which was under the occupation of the ARSK and had been living as refugees in Vodice. From 12 October 1991 to 13 June 1992, the witness was a member of the 113th HV Sibenik Brigade. Later, in 1992, he joined the 15th Home Guard Regiment until he was demobilised prior to Operation Storm. On the eve of Operation Storm, the witness learned that members of the 15th Home Guard were gathering for Storm, so he went to the assembly point with his own uniform and to join the fight. When Operation Storm commenced on the morning of 4 August 1995, his squad was deployed in on Velika Glava, on the site called the graveyard, and made no advancements that day due to the strong resistance from the direction of Gracac. They were ordered to withdraw to their initial positions and started a new attack on 5 August at noon, in which they made advances in the direction of Kistanje. He arrived in Kistanje on 6 or 7 August. At that time, there was no visible sign of damage on the houses. From Kistanje, the witness moved on in the direction of Ivosevci. In Ivosevci they captured the injured and injured ARSK soldier and turned him over to the Medical Corps. They also captured around ten people wearing civilian clothes, but who were armed, and turned them over to the military police. Subsequently, they moved along in that direction until they met up with the members of the 4th Guards Brigade north of Knin. The following day, the witness was in Knin which appeared to be undamaged expect for a house at the base of the fort. The witness then returned to Ivosevci until 18 August when he returned his weapon. After that, the 15th Home Guard went on towards Drvar, but he stayed Ivosevci with some other members of the unit until he was apprehended by the police for the killing of Dara Milosevic in September. The witness was tried, convicted, and sentenced to eight years of imprisonment for murder which was reduced by the Supreme Court to seven years and six months. The witness testified that during the entire time of being a member of the HV and therefore during Operation Storm, he never received an order which would require him to commit a criminal offence. Further, it was his opinion that commanders and the people who trained him abided by international law. That is the summary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now without discussing the matters that were discussed in your report, sir, I want to talk to you about the period of time after Operation Storm. And, Mr. Bilic, were you involved in criminal activity after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And who arrested you when you got arrested?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: The military police arrested me and handed me over to the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, I'd like to show you a -- your arrest report and interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could bring this up. It's 65 ter 1D2739.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is an Official Note of your arrest, Mr. Bilic, of 11 September 1995. Have you seen this before, sir?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I may have. I don't remember. Probably. Probably back in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll offer into evidence 1D2738.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that becomes Exhibit D1548.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bilic, looking at this statement, at the -- approximately the third paragraph from the top it talks about you finding -- being in Kistanje and finding a handgun in the house of an owner of Serbian ethnicity. Is that accurate, sir? Did you find a gun in a Serb house in Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not only a pistol. I also found his military bag. I don't know what it's official called, the officer's brief-case. And I found some documents in the bag, because he was the commander of a unit, probably in Krkovic or somewhere. I handed it over to the command in Kistanje. I don't know where it ended up. I mean, the document or the documents. I kept the bag, the pistol. And as for their uniforms, there were plenty to be had, and we didn't touch those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you some additional questions concerning these weapons. And as you were going through these locations in Kistanje and elsewhere, how available were weapons in the area, after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: You could find them in every house, weapons, Zoljas, uniforms, if nothing else you would have a hunting rifle. We called them "Ciganka." There wasn't a single house that didn't have any weapons, and I can tell you that I went through dozens of them, house by house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As we go further down on this note, it talks about a location called Bratiskovci. Do you see that, sir? Towards the bottom of the page. I think it's towards the bottom of the -- actually about -- it's underlined. It's about seven lines from the bottom of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it notes that -- that you had this weapon and then stated that the last five or six days you were in Bratiskovci where houses and remains of -- remains of houses and -- with the intention to steal for his needs. Now, is that accurate, sir, were you in Bratiskovci for five or six days prior to that, looking to steal for your needs?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Bratiskovci. I was there on that day. I wasn't there for six days -- I was -- on the day when the police arrested me. However, Slobodan Burukalo [phoen] - he was a footballer in the second league in Zagreb; he is from Bratiskovci - and I went to see his grandmother and he -- and she told me that I should take the tractor so that other Ustashas would not take them because that's how they referred to us Croats. We referred to them as Chetniks, I mean, to the Serbs. She gave me the tractor and she gave me some bread as well. We were friends; we were acquaintances from before the war because of her three sons. Two remained in Croatia and of them left having married elsewhere. I put into the car some ham and wine that she gave me, and, at that point, the police indicated that I should pull over. They thought that I had been stealing. I was together with my brother. Our military police took me to Sibenik for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: They knew at that point that Dara had been killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll get to this just step by step if we can, Mr. Bilic, and let's take first things first. Now, this is it the 11th of September, 1995. After Operation Storm and after the period of time of conflict, did you and your other friends begin to drink alcohol frequently.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, we drank non-stop. The only food there was a prosciutto and then there was wine. They were thirsty and we were drunk around the clock. That was the situation. There was euphoria, there was liberation after five years of being refugees. We had been looted, robbed, members of my family were killed. After all that, we simply felt that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's stay with that. When you went back there with your friends -- with your other colleagues and you were drinking, did you go back there to try to exact revenge for what happened to the Croats between 1991 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think a proper way would be, Why did you go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were going into Bratiskovci, why did you go back into those areas? You told us you -- you were meeting a friend there, but did you have any other reasons to go back into Bratiskovci or any of these other villages?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: We had 1001 reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't if we want to hear 1001, because you might be here for a while, but just give us the primary reasons for why you went back.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: My village was surrounded by the Serb villages such as Lisane, Krkovic, Pedancovci [phoen]. So the Croatian villages were surrounded by the Chetnik or Serb villages, whatever you want to call them. Everything that had been stolen from us, starting with our chicken, tractors, livestock, equipment, appliances ... I was from a poor family, a village family, but we had 18 sheep, two cows, two calves, an Arsis [phoen] tractor. We had wine and prosciutto and were left without anything. Even the stone from the walls of the house was taken away. They cut down the trees, killed off everything. We lost our identity, our pride, everything, but we regained it through Operation Storm. Unfortunately, at the time, we were a bit euphoric, there was alcohol; and in the air you could feel smoke, the smell of gun powder. We were drunk and then you start recalling things. And as we were passing through the territory, people would see their old tractor, or old cow, old this and that. That was the context. If our intention had been to kill everyone off, we would have done that right at the outset. I'm sorry to have been and done there, but I can tell you that from the place where I sit now I probably would not act the same way again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, when you went into these villages, did you go into Serb houses and take things out of those houses? Did you loot those houses?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: We did not loot. I was most of the time from -- with the Urukala [phoen] family; I know them from before. Her grandson boxed with me in Zagreb in the Metalac club. We even visited before the war, we played soccer together, we all knew each other. We used to hang out in the summer. We would join soccer tournaments, swim in Vodice. Therefore, I never went to the house of people I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, you said that you didn't loot but you told us earlier that you went in and you were told to take a tractor because you didn't wanted somebody else to get it. The tractor that you took, was that your tractor?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: No, it was that woman's tractor. She told me this: Son, take this. Better you than some other Ustashas. Because they referred to all of us as Ustashas. Then she said, They come daily visiting. And by that time civilians started coming into the territory, since a few days passed after Operation Storm. She said, You should take it rather than someone else. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you and your friends -- excuse me, let me rephrase that. When you went walking through these villages, did you and your friends find things you thought belonged to you?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: As I was returning from the lady's home, I wasn't -- I was alone. But on the way, I met two friends from the village along the road. They saw a small tractor by the side of the road. They asked me to help them load some stuff in my car, and then I towed the tractor with my vehicle. And there was also a trailer on which we put another tractor. We took all of that home -- took all of that home. It was quite an ordinary thing to do at the time. However, later on, there was some interrogation of certain guys from the village concerning the murders in Varivode, and they gathered all those who took part in those operations. They also questioned some of my guys, who were weaklings, slapped once or twice by a policemen. They start immediately talking about the theft of a lamb or a tractor and this and that, and that's how they got to the tractor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilin, the time-frame you're talking about when you're going into these houses with your friends and taking things that they think belong to them, what's time-frame for this? When are you doing this?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, but that was after the operation. The real warriors moved on. I could not, because I had problems with my leg, which had been operated. I still have certain problems walking because my leg hurts, but I wanted to walk into this courtroom for the general to see me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, the question simply was time-frame, not what happened to your leg although that might be important for you. It was not in direct relation to the question. In relation to the start of Operation Storm, was it one day after that, three days after that, a week, two weeks, a month? Could you tell us when this happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some time later. 20 days after Operation Storm more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And are you now talking about being questioned by the police, or are you talking about what you told us about the tractor, which was towed and other tractor being loaded? Which of the two are you talking about, if you say it was 20 days after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the village where I was, it all took place within one, two, or three days, concerning me and the bad things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the story with the tractors found at the side of the road and being questioned by the police, all within three days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More or less. There were a few days of me being drunk and those events taking place. I couldn't be in the field for long because later on I started visiting doctors and I went to Zagreb to have my knee operated on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that other things happened after that. So, altogether, taking your answers together, it was by the end of August, approximately, that it happened, what you told us. Now one question that was put to you was whether you found things you thought that belonged to you. And then you told us about these tractors, that you saw some people you knew, that they asked you to help. Now, what belonged -- or what did you think belonged to you, or was it that they thought that it belonged to them? Could you tell us now, what did you find that you thought belonged to you, or they thought belonged to them? Was it the tractor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember such details anymore. That was a banal thing. I simply cannot recall it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, but you were asked whether you found things you thought belonged to you, and your answer was yes. Now, what exactly did you find that you thought belonged to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. I don't remember what I said in my statement what belonged to me. I only know that the tractor I got that I had with me did not belong to me but that lady of my friend gave it to me. She said that I should take it rather than someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you say, since then it belonged to you. That's clear. Mr. Kehoe, please proceed, and let's try to stick to the facts and primarily facts in relation to answers rather than other facts, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just -- Mr. Bilic, in addition to you, did your friends find things that they thought belonged to them, like livestock or TVs or appliances that they took?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: They did. They told me they recognised lots of their stuff. And this was not just my immediate circle of friends but my whole village; its inhabitants found things in other villages. This person found his or her cow; another person found his tractor. They also recognised some chicken because we used to breed this particular type of chicken in our village. There were many small things and people would recognise them and take them home. I didn't think it was anything special about it at the time. Because all of it was actually ours. It had been taken from us. Later on, we saw those things passing through other villages. We saw many things from our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, let's go forward in this and talk about the police. I mean, did the police, you know, try to stop you and your friends and people that you knew from taking these items?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. But they couldn't. They were powerless, to tell you the truth. This was such a large area. We knew every foot of it. We knew the paths through woods, and they only had check-points along the main roads, the military and civilian police. But that's a Karst area. They are woods there, and we could always find a way without anyone seeing us. We would avoid the check-points, and we would simply take wine or prosciutto. The police were helpless both the MPs and civilian police. There was also UNPROFOR at some check-points, such as at Djevrska and elsewhere. But we always found our way. There this was a large area. Even if they had one policeman for every soldier, still, they wouldn't be able to do that. There were not enough police at the time, and it could not be stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me shift gears and subjects with you, and I'd like that to you about the Dara Milosevic murder and first addressing ourselves to your police statement.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is the questioning of you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we go to the second page of this. Actually, I think it will probably start at the bottom of the -- top of the second page in English, and it starts at the bottom of the second page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it reads that: "As for the murder in the hamlet of Pavici in the village of Bribir he stated that he knows nothing about that. And that he does not know where this happened." Now, when you told the police that on the 11th of September, 1995, that wasn't true; was it?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, and I lied. I didn't even think it was so important. I think it was quite an ordinary thing for that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know if we want to catch up, I have just been reminded by Mr. Misetic that on page 15, line 15, the transcript missed "how many of his family members were killed between 1991 and 1995."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's good to have it on the record. You said your family members were killed between 1991 and 1995 and apparently you gave a number. How many of your family members were killed during those four years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I recalled some other names yesterday evening. I said eight but, unfortunately, there were more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many there were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I go one by one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, if you first give the number. I think it's for an impression. That would do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me count them. Around ten. Immediate and extended family. Because we were all related in one way or another. Uncles, aunts. We were all relatives in that village. Some people had their heads cut off and thrown into wells. Four soldiers were killed during the first attack on the village, when the army and Chetniks entered it. In the very attack, they killed those guys who stayed behind. They killed three or four young guys, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we were just seeking clarification of the number of members of your family that were killed, and that has been clarified. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could bring up 65 ter 1D2770. And this is a report concerning Mr. Bilic and his arrest, and, for the record, Mr. President, this is from a larger document which is 65 ter 1D1244.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bilic, if we could go to page 2 of this document in the report. This is a report of you in the Dara Milosevic murder. And in the second paragraph it notes that you were in -- that sometime between 6 September 1995 and 7 September 1995 you went to Pavici. Is that about right, sir, that you went to Pavici?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And why did you go to Pavici, sir?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I didn't go to Pavici, but I was simply passing through. That was the first time I went through Pavici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. But --

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So what was the purpose of you stopping and going to that location? Were you going to visit somebody, were you doing something? Why did you stop there?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: No. I went this with the commander of another platoon, from Urocevci [phoen]. They were guarding the -- what do you call it? The pipelines, water -- water ways, whatever. They were guarding the church, the religious monuments up there, and so on. As he was going back home, I encountered him because I was going up to see them because my guys were up there as well. As we were going back, we stopped in Pavici, because there was heavy rain that day, so we were there by accident, by chance. We noticed a man whom I knew. This is it Zdravcina; he is a Chetnik, one of the organisers back in 1995 he slapped my father. I recognised him. The guy I was with was Jakov Vucenovic, he was a teacher by vocation. And I told him, You were a calmer person than I am. Go and ask Dara. I knew all of them, the late Dara's son was in the 5th Regiment. Therefore my intention was not to kill her. I could have done that right away. My plan was to capture the Chetnik alive, the organiser from Bribirske Mostine. He was one of the participants of the so-called log revolution. They stopped us at one point on the road because we went up to their village to get water. That was the only village which had a source of water, a lake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let me stop you there, sir. I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we try to get -- there are a lot of reference because my guys were up there. Who are "my guys"? Could you please try to keep the story a bit structured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me focus you, Mr. Bilic. What were you doing in Dara Milosevic's house?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I waited for the Chetnik known as Zdravcina. Because I saw him up there. I wasn't in the house but behind the house. I waited for him for three nights, not during the day. I wanted to capture him alive to learn some things because my best friend and relative, Perisa Borislav, is still missing after an operation in Dragisa. Ten of our soldiers were captured. Two of which were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Croatian soldiers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go back to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, could we first try to find out where this Pavici is, for example, just to start with, so that we know what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This village of Pavici, where you killed Dara Milosevic, where is that?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Close to Bribirske Mostine and my village. It's all within a distance of five to six kilometres. I attended school --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... before we go to the whole of the education, could you assist us -- and perhaps parties could agree on where Pavici is then so that we know what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, maybe in map number 25 in our court booklet which is now P2427. It's in the municipality of Skradin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Skradin is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: South of Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Skradin, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the wider village of Bribirske is slightly north-west in that municipality and Pavici is a smaller village. That's the way we understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's approximately right. If we would go to Kistanje, it is it close to a village -- well, not far from Djevrska. If we go to Kistanje it is down the road, I guess, it would be south-west.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: South-west that's in the direction of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Djevrska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. If we go a little further from Djevrska, it's further south-west of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you please repeat the number of the map at this moment in evidence so that I could...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. It's P2427. And I would have a more detailed map of the area for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have one and if it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It can be put onto the ELMO. I also have a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you look at this map, P2427, the Sibenik municipality, you can see the municipality of Skradin and then you have the name of Skradin underlined and the village of Bribir is about two centimetre above the word Skradin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And little village of Pavici is just slightly north of Bribir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The village itself is not any of these maps. But that's the location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then at least we know where we are moving around and also where Krkovic is, which ... Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, do you see where Krkovic is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Krkovic is the place where the witness -- he was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I understand that's his birthplace, that's where he's from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's where he is from. Yes, I see that the distance. The distance between the village where he is from is relatively small, yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, just for clarity sake, how far is the village where you are from, Krkovic, from Pavici and Dara Milosevic's house, approximately? Distance.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Between Krkovic and Bribirske Mostine, there is two and a half to three kilometres. That's where the main school was for all the surrounding villages. Now Bribirske Mostine and Pavici are perhaps a kilometre apart. So in all, three to four kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine. Let's go back to the question we asked before. Why were you in Dara Milosevic's house?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I already said that as I was on my way through the village, I saw the individual who, back in 1991, slapped my father about. As we were going passed his house, on our way to the main springs, water springs, that's where we would normally get water supplies and we would transport them by tractors. It was in 1991 in June or July --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: -- that they had already erected barricades and stopped my father and me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand that you noted for us that this man slapped your father back in 1991. Now, tell us in -- in September of 1995, why were you in Dara Milosevic's house? What were you doing in her house?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I wanted to capture him alive. That was the reason why I was there, not for one day, but for three days or, rather, evenings. On the fourth evening, I heard somebody talking in the house, and subsequently the police told me that in fact it was the lady, the woman who was intoxicated, talking to herself, and I was convinced that it was him with her. She was baking bread, and food was plentiful in the house. You see, previously, Mr. Vucenovic, whom I mentioned, and I had talked to the woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... when you got in the house, what did you do with regard to the killing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question before that. What was the relation between the person you were looking for and that lady?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. I do know that he was seen. She was baking bread, and she could not have been baking for her sake alone. She was alone in the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said you do not know what the relationship is. If I'm looking for Mr. X, why would I go to the house of lady Y? What made you believe that he might be there in that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because we saw him previously. On that particular day, that we saw him, we weren't able to capture him because there was heavy rain. It was within five minutes that the teacher arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where did you see him? At the house of this lady?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In front of the house. He was talking to her, and I'm sure of that. 100 per cent, or million per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And because it was raining you didn't go after him although he was there alone with the old lady or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to explain. Since I am quite hot-tempered, and especially so in his regard, I asked the teacher who was an older man, Jakov Vucenovic, he was a teacher in the high school, and I asked him, Please, go and see the old lady and ask her where he was to be found at that point. Whereas we, for our part, parked the car a bit further away from the house. He went to the house and asked her, Grandma, who was it who spoke to you five minutes ago? You see that? All it took place in the span ever five minutes. She replied in the dialect that they usually speak in, No, no, I'm telling for a fact I wasn't talking to him. So she wouldn't admit. And then I said, Well, who gives a shit about her. Let's go away, and I'll catch him sometime. So we left. We left home. However, at around 7.00 or 8.00 p.m. on that same day, there was this bar in Vodice where all the soldiers would gather in the evening, socialise, et cetera. Several soldiers among them said that they had met Zdravcina, the person I was looking for. I asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave you, now, further in the hands of Mr. Kehoe who will try to get the story as factual as possible and also in such a way that it becomes logically presentable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, on that score, if could ask the intelligence of Your Honour and counsel if I could lead through this to a degree so we can get through this as expeditiously as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, you went back to this house in Pavici with a gun to find this Serb that you were looking for, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you sat and waited for him for three day, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Three nights, yes, not during the day. There was no point in being there during the day, because, you see, behind the house there was a forest where they hid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. And you went there to exact revenge against this man for slapping your father, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The question that has been asked, I agreed to a certain leading in terms of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In factual terms, and perhaps not in terms of motive. Is that what --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you do that in terms of motive, sir? Is that why you want back there, to exact revenge from this man for slapping your father?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't want to take revenge. I wanted him alive. I wanted him to tell me everything and he must have known everything. He was the chief organiser together with several other individuals from the village who I know very, very well, and who I saw holding guard at the time, when Ugljesa, the restaurant owner, was killed. The second one --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: -- was alive and where as Zdravcina, I wanted to get hold of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously the witness answered his motives for the -- the Chetnik he was looking for. So if the follow-up question is what his motives are for killing the women, that should be asked in a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... going into that. I'm trying to take it, counsel, as sequentially as I possibly can with the leading so we can get through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Facts, no problem as far as leading is concerned. Subjective considerations not to be asked in a leading way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, were you drunk when you went to this house and shot Dara Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember. I was probably under the influence of alcohol to some extent, although I was quite strong and could hold my alcohol. I wanted to catch him alive, and he was my target. It was not my intention to kill the woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, did anybody in the HV order to you go to that house to try to capture this man, or did you do this on your own?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: On my own. I asked certain -- young men to come along and help me, but they were cowards. I wanted to catch him, so I went on my own. Unfortunately, what I didn't want either happened. The lady -- the woman was drunk and she was talking to herself in the house. It was on that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: -- third or fourth night, I don't remember. So I barged into the house --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, sir. Now let's take this slower. When you went there on the day that Dara Milosevic was shot, were you wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat what he said about the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you repeat what you just said about wearing the uniform.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: A black uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you went in there at night, you shot Dara Milosevic. Tell the Court why you shot Dara Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I didn't want to shoot her. This was a coincidence. It was a combination of circumstances. I thought I heard her talk to someone, but she was not. I only learned later that she was talking to herself. She was shouting. It was only later on when I was already in detention that the police told me that she was prone to drinking, roaming the village, and shouting. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I barged into the house --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You barged into the house and you shot this woman and did you --

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Not that way, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let's take it step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You barged into that house. What did you see? How many persons did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was night-time, around 3.00 or 4.00 a.m. I was convinced that the Chetnik was inside with her and that they were quarrelling and talking, so I barged into the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not asking you what you were convinced of. My question was: What did you see. You said it was dark. Was there any light in the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No light in the house. Did you hear, at that moment, when you were in the house, anyone talking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not in the house. I was behind the house, holding guard, standing guard. I don't know how to put it, for three evenings. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- all one could hear throughout the time was silence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you, when you went into the house, you said you couldn't see anyone because of the darkness. Was there no light? Is that what was the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is not quite correct. I would formulate it differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tell me how I would have to formulate my questions. Factual. What --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was summertime, so it was already dusk. It was getting lighter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At 3.00 or 4.00 a.m., you already have the crack of dawn, and it was becoming lighter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say there was already some light. What did you see when you entered that house? Did you see any human being?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I kicked the door open quite swiftly and said, Ustasha, who are you talking to? But then I realized that I only saw her and nobody else with her, but she was upon me, at that point, shouting already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You went into that house and you saw a human being. You, sir, saw her. Did you see anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did you say to her? Shout or say or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I said something like, Ustasha, who are you talking to? And she frightened -- she was frightened at that point and she pushed me back because I fired at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... take it step by step. So you said, Ustasha, who are you talking? Did she respond with words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She said, Yes, you, Ustasha devil, get out of my house. Something like that. You see, they have this Serbian accent which is somewhat different. I fired the weapon without thinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was the time between coming into the house and firing at the deceased, the person that deceased. Was it one second, was it three seconds, was it ten seconds? Just try to remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can visualize it, although I'm trying to push that memory away. As I stormed into the house, I immediately shouted, Who are you talking to? At that point I realized that it was only a small room that I got into because I couldn't picture the layout of the house from the outside. I thought it was a bit larger. No, it was a small room, and I said Cetnikusa, who are you talking to? And she said, you Ustasha devil. And that's when I fired a shot. I don't know if I did it deliberately or inadvertently. I just fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... talking about a matter of seconds. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, of course. It was a matter of seconds. I didn't think about it. This thought "I'm going to kill you" didn't cross my mind. Besides, her son served in the military together with me, the military term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just talking about whether it was a matter of seconds. Mr. Kehoe, sorry for interrupting, but I would like it know what the facts are. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, thereafter, sir, and let me go back to your -- this report, which is 1D2770, you were stopped on the 9th of September, according to this report, and the weapon that you had killed Dara Milosevic was taken from you; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in the last paragraph, the police authorities matched that weapon to the bullet that was taken from Dara Milosevic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2770.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1549.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just finish one last document before Your Honour takes a break, if I may, it will be quite brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One more question on the previous issue: When you entered into that house, do you remember whether the lady was standing, was sitting, was -- was there a table, was there a chair, was there a bed in that room? Could you describe the furniture of that room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She was on her feet. It was a small room. I think it only had a bed and a cupboard. I only glanced a second at the room itself and then I immediately went out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring up 1D2771.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the speaker, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 1D -- 65 ter 1D2771. This is the -- the judgement as well -- of the trial court, as well as the appellate court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, you were, in fact, tried and convicted of murder, were you not?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you were initially sentenced to eight years in prison and on appeal that was reduced to seven and a half years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2771, which is taken from a larger OTP document, 65 ter 3926.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1550.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Kehoe, is it your intention to go into the enforcement of the sentence as well or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not. Then I'd like to ask: Did you serve your sentence, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In full?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much did you serve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President Tudjman pardoned me, and this happened, I don't know which year it was. And then I -- my sentence was reduced by two years. And then again in 1998 for the Croatian national holiday my sentence was once more reduced by two years so that all in all, thanks to my good conduct and my ill health, I was released after serving three and a half years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's in paragraph 5 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would have gone into it had I not been there, Mr. President, but at the risk of duplicating --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes, I -- no that was -- I overlooked that. Yes, I -- you're perfectly right, Mr. Kehoe, I should have remembered that. This is a duplication and now there's some exchange money for you, as far as duplication is concerned. Anything else before the break, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Not before the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break, and we will resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. I'll be referring to without putting these up on the screen at this point, Mr. President, consistent with Your Honours' ruling yesterday concerning Official Notes of third parties. I would be looking at 65 ter 1D2735, counsel, and 65 ter 1D2736.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic do you have an individual by the name of Barislav Djeranic [sic]?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think the name is Serkanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Serkanic, excuse me. You're absolutely right, Serkanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Berislav Serkanic. Do you know that individual?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that he gave several police statements to the Ministry of the Interior police, the MUP police, where he noted that you took part in a rape in Gorice, the village of Gorice?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I learned that later on. He is a pathological liar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, were you in fact in this woman's house that -- when she was sexually assaulted?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I was, but she was not sexually assaulted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was this woman a Serb?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. It all took place in the course of those few days. As I have just said, in the five years of being drunk and -- in the five days of being drunk and mad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And who were you with at that time, when you were at this woman's house?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: The trial took place not so long ago, but I forgot. There were two or three guys. I didn't usually hang out with them, but it just so happened that evening that I did. I was with my car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you with Ante Matic?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Nikola Bilic?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Neno Bilic?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Stipe Perisa?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I think he was there. Or, no, I don't know. I can't recall. The trial took place only recently. But these guys are -- were not my regular crowd. They are friends of mine and acquaintances and distant relatives from the village, but they were not at my level in terms of soldiering, and they were not my friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, were you charged and convicted for this sexual assault?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And were you sentenced? And, if so, what sentence did you receive?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, the sentence is one year of treatment ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer. It was inaudible and incomprehensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, could you repeat the last answer. And when I asked you, Were you sentenced, and if so, what sentence did you receive. Could you repeat your answer again?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I got one year of jail of being under supervision and treatment in the hospital prison, the prison in Sveta Simonska Street. I don't know what the name of it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what is the status of that case right now? Where is that case?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I haven't even received the first-instance court judgement. This was completed perhaps a month or a month and a half ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, the night when you were in this woman's house with these other individuals, were they wearing uniforms that night?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. The trial was just recently. I don't remember. I didn't pay much attention to such detail. Maybe they were, maybe they were not. I don't remember. I really can't say. I told that to the court, and maybe you have the judgement with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were they armed? Did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the judgement final?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My understanding it is on appeal at this point so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Shouldn't we then -- you are always so cautious in reminding witnesses that if the true answers to the questions might incriminate them, that they are not under a duty to answer those questions unless ordered to do so. This case is not over yet. It may be that truthful answers to the questions put to you by Mr. Kehoe might -- may incriminate yourself. If that is the case, you can refuse to answer the question. Although, this Chamber could order you, nevertheless, to answer that question. Of course, we do not know. But you are the first one to say, If I would answer this question in accordance with the truth, I might incriminate myself. That's what you have to raise, if that applies. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, just a few more questions on this incident. Were you wearing a uniform that night? Did you understand --

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I think I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did anyone from the Croatian army order you or any of the individuals that were present to go to that Serb woman's house that night?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, subject to Your Honours' ruling yesterday with regard to Official Notes that -- well, not this individual's Official Notes. We will at this point MFI 1D2735 as well as 1D2736.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber awaits your submissions by the end of this week. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, those will become Exhibit D1551 and Exhibit D1552, respectively, both marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this point, I have no further questions. Mr. Bilic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Any questions for this witness by the Cermak Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No questions from us, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will now be cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Bilic.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you for a clarification. In paragraph 4 of your statement, which has become D1547, you say that the enemy offered strong resistance from the direction of Gracac and the road between Pavasovici and Gracac. Can you tell us where Gracac is, the place that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: From Skradin first you get into the village of Pavasovici where the Croatian army was. From Pavasovici to Gracac there was a road which was no man's land. There was a line of separation there. Gracac is the first Serb village stronghold that they were supposed to take over in Operation Storm. Unfortunately, we didn't succeed that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So Gracac is close to Skradin?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know of another Gracac in Lika?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's a completely different place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, are you ready to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Waespi. Mr. Waespi is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We do agree that this is a different Gracac. The one the witness referred is also contained in P2427.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, even prior to Operation Storm you had a heavy criminal record; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 3926. And this is in e-court -- it's a large document, but in e-court it's pages 43 to 44, two pages. And in English it's the first translation that's linked to this 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that if you later want to tender this it is just these two page us that want to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bilic, I counted eight judgements, sentences, convictions of you of various heavy crimes like aggravated theft, damaging property, participation in a brawl, which you committed between 1976 and 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is all correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you were sentenced on many of these occasions to fines and several prison sentences, some of them over a year, and the highest one two years and two months; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I guess so. I no longer remember. I pushed that back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I think you once told the public prosecutor, Mr. Zganjer, that, prior to Operation Storm, you spent altogether four to five years in prison?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And prior to Operation Storm, you had a treatment in a psychiatric clinic in Sibenik; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now let's go to the moment when you went into the 15th Home Guard Regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, do you want to tender the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2561.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: First of all, I believe you testified or it's part of your witness statement that already in 1992 and 1993 you were part of the 15th Home Guard Regiment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe in your witness statement you told the Defence that, already, in 1992 or 1993 you were a part of the 15th Home Guard Regiment. It's in paragraph 1 of your statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in 1995, and we see that from your witness statement, paragraph 3, you say that, and I quote: "I was informed that members of the 15th DP were gathering for Storm. Given that my cousin informed me of this and I went to the Krka falls where the mobilisation assembly point was located and there were already two or 3.000 soldiers there. I was issued with a weapon in Skradin. I was issued with an automatic rifle and I had my own uniform." Now, did somebody take down your name when you joined the 15th Home Guard Regiment? Can you explain, how was the process of you enlisting or becoming a member of that unit look like?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: It was simple. In Skradin, there was the command post of the 15th Home Guards Regiment. There was also a warehouse where one got weapons. I remember a guy by the name Sladic who was there. He was the main man in the warehouse. I was issued with a weapon, the so-called "Ciganka" rifle and about a dozen of us that could board a truck were sent to the Krka falls. We spent the night there, and we waited for the attack at dawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bilic, who sent you to the Krka falls; do you remember the person?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: No. We gathered there. There were lots and lots of people, thousands upon thousands. I don't know the name of a person. I would be saying silly things if I tried to tell you any names. I came there as a volunteer. I had been retired by the time. On the 26th of October of 1995 I received my pension. I submitted a request, and I was supposed to be retired. I went to Storm voluntarily. Since my cousin was a communications Sergeant, he called us in Vodice to tell us to put our families in the basement because they expected there would be counter-shelling by Chetniks. That's what we did. We went to see our parents in the hotel, and I went then to Skradin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in that truck on which you boarded to go to the Krka falls, how many soldiers were on that truck, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
