utterances.text: Perhaps around a dozen guys. But trucks kept going and cars were there as well. There was a lot of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And these people on -- on the -- on the truck, they were all soldiers like you?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were all soldiers. And mostly volunteers. My guys were volunteers. I gathered a group of volunteers. These were all people I knew from before. My commander asked -- not my commander but the commander of the battalion asked for the bravest guys, two or three platoons, who would commence an attack from two or three different sides in the morning. And I chose a squad for myself. He knew me from before as a soldier, and he approved. He approved that I choose about a dozen guys. I chose those I deemed the best.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. And this battalion commander is known to you as Kova by nickname. Is that the person?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember his rank?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: He commanded the battalion. But before that, he did not command my battalion. I used to be with another battalion in Vodice. He was in Skradin. So we went in the field as needed. I was part of the interventions -- intervention platoon in Vodice. Whenever there was a need to intervene, I underwent training in several different camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you're talking about 1995, that you were a part of the intervention squad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: No, before, while I was part of the regular army. In 1995, I volunteered to participate in Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Let's stick to 1995. I'll ask you specifically when I want to hear information about the years prior to that. So, it was in --

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- it was in 1995 that your battalion commander asked you to pull together --

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- a squad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that was not so. He asked a soldier of his, an active-duty soldier he commanded - who, in terms of rank, was somewhat junior to him, I believe - but Commander Kova was preoccupied gathering troops in Skradin. But in the morning, at an around 3.00 before the attack he said, Guys, if any of you is not brave enough, do not even get up. Otherwise, I need three platoons of volunteers, three platoons of 30 men strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. And you said this Kova knew you from before the war or from -- before Operation Storm; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: No. I knew him from the war. We all knew each other. Skradin is a small place. The 15th Regiment, we all know each other not by first or last names but in passing. I was rather specific. I stood out because I took part in different operations on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Kova, your battalion commander, did he know that you were a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Of course, he did. I was not the only one. There were thousands of volunteers there. Even children and women wanted to go, but they were not allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did -- I think I asked you this question before, but you may not have answered. Did somebody take down your name in that warehouse when you were issued your rifle?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I told you they did, but I can't remember anyone's name. I think it was this Sladic, the warehouse keeper, of the warehouse in Skradin where the weapons depot was. I was issued with a "Ciganka" rifle, that's how we called it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now you mentioned in your statement that your unit incurred losses. I think you mentioned one killed and six wounded after you had passed the village of Pavasovici and then you were ordered to withdraw. Do you recall who gave you the order to withdraw?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't. But I was Zabac-3 that was my communications code. I heard the message to retreat. At that point, I was to the right of Pavasovici and the road. I heard a lot of firing and the Chetniks put up resistance. I think they even used a Bofors anti-aircraft machine-guns. A guy was killed in the middle of the road. I didn't know that at that point, but I learned that later in Skradin. I was on the side next to the graveyard a few hundred metres away from where the guy was killed and the other six wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And with whom were you in communications with? You said had you a -- a radio. Who was among the group you were talking to?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know who was in charge of operations. Perhaps the chief commander. I don't know. Someone did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, to whom would you talk on your radio or receive messages from?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: My code-name was Zabac-3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes I understand. Who was Zabac-1?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe it was Pavasovici, someone on the right-hand side, I don't know. We moved in from several different directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who was Pavasovici?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: No, the village of Pavasovici. It was a Serb village where the Croatian army was. Between Pavasovici and Gracac. The distance was one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Witness. So you did communicate with some other members of your unit, whether on your level, or perhaps with your company. Is that a fair assessment of with whom you were communicating on the radio?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know with whom. Someone who was in charge of the operation, and I don't know who it was. I was just a soldier. My goal was to go via Velika Glava and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Let's talk about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Most of the locations mentioned, I haven't an idea of where to find them. Velika Glava, is however ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is it close to the Mijanovici higher up and also somewhere above Skradin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But still in that same area, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the separation line, at Velika Glava. The so-called "cemetery." Sometimes they would re-gain that territory, and then we would offer a counterattack and it changed hands five or six times. That was the main elevation. If they controlled that, they could enter Skradin. Therefore, that was an important point for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Close do Skradin at the confrontation line. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move on to a second location that you mentioned in your evidence-in-chief and this relates to paragraph 4 of your witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we can pull up D1547, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bilic, in -- in your witness statement towards the end of paragraph 4 you elaborate on the location of the 15th Home Guard Regiment in the aftermath of Operation Storm, and it relates to the village of Ivosevci. And let me read what you told the Defence: "I stayed in Ivosevci until 18 August" --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's on page 2 of the English version just above paragraph 5. Second page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'll start reading. I'm sure we can find it on the second page in -- in English. If there's a cover page, it's the third page; I apologise for that. End of paragraph 4, just before paragraph 5. Let me read: "I stayed in Ivosevci until 18 August when I returned my weapon and was demobilised?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, a second, counsel. It's the next page in English for the reading part. It's at the top of the next page, the carry-over paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and halfway the first paragraph in English. I think we now moved the B/C/S, but we should have moved the English only. If we move a little bit more to the left we can see the paragraph numbering in English as well. Yes, there we are. No, it's paragraph 4 from what I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Just the end of paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me start again: "I stayed in Ivosevci until 18 August when I returned my weapon and was demobilised. My unit went on toward Drvar, but I stayed in Ivosevci with some other members of the 15th Home Guard Regiment and carried out tasks that were assigned with -- we were assigned with. I had a weapon even after the demobilisation, and I remained in the area of Ivosevci and continued to participate in carrying out tasks to the best of my abilities. This continued until I was apprehended." Now let's briefly have a look at the location of the village of Ivosevci.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, this it P2423 or map 21 in your court binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bilic, this village, Ivosevci is just above Kistanje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe we can see it -- the actual town of Kistanje, not the name of the municipality. It's north-east of Kistanje; that's the village of Ivosevci. Is that the village we're talking about, Mr. Bilic?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, what are these tasks that you and other members remaining behind of the 15th Home Guard Regiment had to carry out?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Let me start from the beginning, from the point when we reached Kistanje, and then on to Ivosevci --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm actually not interested -- I'm not interested in what happened in Kistanje. I'm interested in -- when the gross of the 15th Home Guard Regiment moved onwards to Drvar you said you stayed behind in this village and received tasks. Can you tell us as brief as you can what these tasks were.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: We were guarding the water tower, a large water-tower located beyond Kistanje. There were two churches there as well, and we were arresting the Chetniks that -- who remained behind. Some ten days later, we noticed that cows were provided need in troughs, and we knew that it couldn't have been women who did that. Let me illustrate this. We would come across a trough which was used for cows to take water from, and we knew that there was some 50 cow heads in the area. Our assessment was that there must have been men around that we never came across, since we only saw elderly people and women. We, the Croatian soldiers, wanted to waylay them in the early morning hours, and that's where we captured them, in fact. It's a forested area. It's a very high forest, sticking two metres above our heads. And this is where we captured them. Some of them guarded the church in Kistanje, others guarded the approach roads, et cetera. Most of the lads went on to engage in subsequent fighting. I had -- my knee was giving me trouble. I had water in my knee, and I had attended on several occasions in Vodice so I couldn't join them, although I wanted to very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I understand that. Who gave you these tasks, to guard the -- the church and the other tasks you just outlined? Was there somebody specific who told you what to do every morning?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't recall the names of the commanders of platoons that were there. I came there as a volunteer. What's more, I was the one who ordered that the church be guarded. I was the morale commander, so to speak, when we were in Kistanje; and it was on the same night that we reached Ivosevci. When I was in Kistanje, and this is something that the Croatian TV filmed and subsequently broadcast as part of their prime news and first news reports from Knin, I -- I said that we were in Kistanje and that was on the 6th or on the 7th in the afternoon, and I said that we were waiting for orders. This was recorded by the Croatian TV. I and a colleague of mine who were the first one to reach Kistanje, not only Kistanje but all the villages from Velika Glava to Kistanje who were interviewed by the TV crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I think part of it is already contained in your witness statement. Let me go back to Ivosevci. You said you were kind of the morale commander. Who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Lads who were more courageous and part of the select few, had already gone on towards Bihac or -- I don't know precisely where. I only know there was a threat of Bihac falling. As for Ivosevci, let me tell you that I don't know the name of the commander, but I know these lads by sight. We all knew each other by sight, not by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the other people who were with you doing these tasks, how many were there; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: There was always ten of us in a group, around ten of us. We would set an ambush for the Chetniks. I mentioned the water trough and the cows. My squad alone captured many of them and handed them over to the police in Bribirske Mostine and to UNPROFOR that was located further down there. They were taking to the Sibenik or Split prison, I don't know where. And then subsequently, it was on Christmas Day in 1995 that Tudjman pardoned them, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you report to anybody the success of your capturing these Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. We handed them over - I will not mince my words - as cattle, but we would call someone from the police located in Bribirske Mostine where had you an UNPROFOR check-point as well as a military and police check-point. And I don't know where they took them, to the prisons in Sibenik or Split. When I was arrested a month later, I met quite a few of them in detention. And if it wasn't unfortunate, it would be funny, when I killed that old woman I -- I met him --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure who.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know how he came to be there, maybe he surrendered to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you mention the name of the person you met of these few who were in detention? Did you just mention the name? Because the interpreter couldn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question now, either, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You earlier said that -- you said it was almost funny that you met someone after had you been arrested. Apparently a person you had earlier --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sought -- when I killed the old woman. Zdravcina. It was him that I met in the Sibenik prison when the police took me into custody. I saw him in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was about the name. It's clear now. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. To --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For my information again, just looking at the maps at this moment, Bribirske Most is -- I'm just trying to orient myself. I think the parties will ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That would be south of -- I understand, but I'm actually not sure myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Certainly. Bribirske, what we were talking about earlier where the killing occurred, that would be south of Kistanje in the Sibenik -- in the Skradin municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just two more questions on this topic, Mr. Bilic. In your squad, were there only volunteers like you, or were there also regular soldiers? And I'm talking about the squad that remained behind in Ivosevci.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you. I'm not sure. I -- I can't assert whether those others were mobilised or volunteers. I only know that those among my lads who were most courageous and the fittest went on to -- toward Drvar. I was unable to. I was not in good health.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did the commanders who went on to Drvar know that a squad was left behind in Ivosevci chasing the Chetniks? Was that known to them?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move on to the murder of Dara Milosevic. And I will not go into details again. But afterwards, after you were -- you had killed Dara Milosevic, you were stopped by the civilian police at a check-point near the hamlet of Gorice, and the police was interested in wine you had with you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could have another excerpt from 65 ter 3926. And in B/C/S this is page 69. And in English this is the translation that's -- I think it's a second translation, which has the ERN 0334-4653, and it's on page 5 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, do you remember that you gave a statement in relation to the murder of Dara Milosevic to the district public prosecutor Zeljko Zganjer on 8th October, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: If I remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go in the English to the first page, and in B/C/S, a couple of pages -- I think it's page 66 in the B/C/S. That's a cover page of this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps the cover page refreshes your memory. Now, I see a record of interview with the accused compiled at the county court in Sibenik on 8 October 1995. And you even have a Defence counsel with you on that day, Frane Baica, attorney-at-law, in Sibenik? Do you remember now that you gave a statement as an accused?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. On the last page, I believe it is signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So let's go again to page 69 in B/C/S, and in English, it's on page 5. And I'll read in English, middle of the second full paragraph, and in B/C/S, it's at the end of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: "I was stopped by the civilian police at a check-point near the hamlet of Gorice. They asked me to hand over the wine to them, but I refused. Since I was wearing a military uniform and considered myself a soldier, they called military police. The military police took me to Sibenik. There they confiscated my pistol and began to question me whether I knew anything about the murder of an old lady in Pavici. They also confiscated my car. When the military police let me go, I began to consider the possibility that I would be found out, but hoped that the investigation would not be very thorough, since the victim was a Serbian woman." Now, turning to that last comment from you to the public prosecutor. What made you expect that the judicial procedures would not be so thorough, given that it was a Serb woman?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: What was I thinking?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. What caused you to tell that to the public prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can only repeat that all those who stayed behind in Krajina voted in favour of Krajina, and they were all Chetniks to me. Those aged 18 and above. There were quite a few Serb civilians who stayed behind in Croatia and defended Croatia; whereas those others, they created their own state there. And I considered all of them to be Chetniks because they had taken my home and my homeland. And all those aged 18 and above were considered Chetniks by me. Just remember Vukovar, Zadar, Sibenik, Gospic, and what they did there. What am I supposed to say to that? Good evening, grandma, what are you doing? Is this what I'm supposed to say after all they've done to us? This was not an act of revenge, it was normal under the circumstances in my mind. What your view of the situation is quite a different matter. At that time, I, as a Croatian soldier; a humiliated person; and my family, we considered them to be enemies up to the point until we liberated. And I was sorry, when Tudjman and the United States, or who it was, stopped us before we reached Banja Luka and on -- Belgrade, and their neck of woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. And --

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- you considered yourself a soldier at that time in early September; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: September? Which month is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: September, that's the month after August. The month in which you killed Dara Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: As a -- strictly speaking, I was no longer a soldier, because I had handed over my soldier [sic]. But, of course, we were under the influence, intoxicated, we wanted to have something to drink. We wanted to have something to eat. We weren't taking something that belonged to them. We were taking back what was ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told the public prosecutor you considered yourself a soldier at that time. You just repeated it --

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Well, fine, I also consider myself to be a Croatian soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And as a soldier, you would have followed any order you were given; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is a word missing in the witness's last answer in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have that first to be completed. You said: "Well, fine, I also consider myself ..." And what did you consider yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're trying to find out what you exactly said. The question that was put to you was: "You told the public prosecutor" -- and Mr. Waespi was referring what you told at the time to the public prosecutor in 1995, "you told that public prosecutor that you considered yourself a soldier." And Mr. Waespi added that's what you just told us now as well. And then your answer started by saying: "Well, fine, I also consider myself ..." And then could you please repeat what you then said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That that was my line of thinking. I didn't think there was anything bad in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But we just want you to repeat what you said. "Well, fine, but I consider myself to be ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm an invalid, a Croatian martyr. If I were asked, I would go and fight again, if I was attacked, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is my assumption right that you do not understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand a single thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take your earphones off for a second. Mr. Misetic, apparently something is still missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe what the witness said was: Well, fine, I consider myself even today a Croatian soldier. So he was saying "today" as we sit in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can confirm that. I also heard that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, any objection if I would try to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Whatever you try to, Mr. President, of course, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, it would be in a rather leading way. You mean to say as long as you try and do not succeed, everything's fine? Mr. Bilic, some in this courtroom thought that you said: "Well, fine, but I consider myself to be a Croatian soldier still to this day." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not in that sense or context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is it what you said, even if it needs a bit of interpretation? Is that what you said a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm always a Croatian soldier. I am a patriot; put it the way you like it. I'm always prepared to go and fight for my country if it is under attack. Even now, officially, of course, I'm not a soldier. I'm a retired Croatian defender, veteran.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I think we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any further need to verify, then it can be done on the basis of the audio. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, during Operation Storm, as a soldier, you followed any orders you were given by your superiors; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I didn't receive that many. I had that main task which was to break through the line and to reach Ivosevci where we were to link up with the 4th Brigade that was coming from the direction of Knin. That was the priority. Whatever came subsequently was taking place on the basis of my assessment. Because I was unable to join the other lads who advanced further, and that's all there is to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you would have certainly accepted any order that came from General Gotovina and followed him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Of course I would. I would have. I would have gone to Drvar or even Belgrade on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to 23rd August, 1995, when you were stopped by the military police driving in a Lada vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is 1D987, a report by the military crime police -- and before that, I would like to tender the previous document, which was 3926B, the 65 ter number, again, only these few pages. Five pages, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was the interview taken by Mr. Zganjer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it clear to Mr. Registrar which pages you're exactly -- I see he is nodding yes. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2562.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask for one second for the witness to take his earphones off again. Could you take your earphones off. Mr. Waespi, you just referred to the 23rd of August. And as you said, when you were stopped by the military police driving in a Lada vehicle. I noticed that two pieces of evidence apparently contradict each other: whether he was stopped by the civilian police and then, because of the uniform, was taken to the military police, or handed over to the military police; or, as we find in his statement of today, and previously referred to the Zganjer statement, which contradicts paragraph 5 of the statement that he was apprehended by members of the military police and was then turned over to the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think there were several instances of the witness being stopped or arrested. I believe after the murder of Dara Milosevic, he was apprehended on the 9th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would say we're now talking about September so we have to clearly distinguish between August and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Exactly. Now I want to go to August, to the 23rd of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I just noticed that I got the impression, but I might be wrong, that what he said to Mr. Zganjer and what we find in paragraph 5 that that's both his arrest in relation to the killing of Dara Milosevic. But I might be wrong, but I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- just sharing my confusion with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe we can clear it up with this exhibit, which is 1D987.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the witness has his earphones on again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I would like read [sic] you from a report by the military crime police dated 14th September 1995. And it relates to you being stopped. Let me read from page 3 in English, and in B/C/S it's also page 3. English, the second paragraph, and B/C/S, one, two, three, the third paragraph. "On 23rd August, 1995, at around 1700 hours at the approach to Vodice, a Lada vehicle with no number plates was stopped. Riding in it were members of the HV VP Sibenik." Now in the B/C/S original it says: "... VP 8287, Sibenik." Which is an indication to the unit. I continue: "Veselko Bilic, son of Tomislav, born on 20 March 1957 in Krkovic, resident in Vodice, Sime Sijca Street number 21, and Mile Colak, son of Rajko, born on 16 February 1951 in Piramatovci, they were carrying a three-seat sofa red and armchair a double bed a small cabinet, a carpet, and four bed covers which they had taken from a village unknown to them in the vicinity of Knin. The items were handed over for safekeeping and a military disciplinary report was filed against the above-mentioned [sic]." Now, Mr. Bilic, is this record of your being stopped at that check-point a correct one, as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So it appears that you were looting in a village near Knin; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: We were not. We took our stuff. The other person mentioned here, well, he simply recognised some of his own stuff, and those items were even returned to him after a while by the police. He lived in Vodice, and he had some papers invoices of some closets and beds. That's what I learned later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And which village did you go to, to pick up these items? Village in the vicinity of Knin?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was it --

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't remember such details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So was Mr. Colak from that village?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know. No, no, not from the village where we took the stuff from. His house was looted. He was from Piramatovci which is next to my village in the same parish. These two villages are connected. Their village was looted as much as mine and he recognised some of his own stuff in the villages above that area. He took that, but when we were stopped by the police those items were taken away, since he could not prove that they were his. However, I learned subsequently that he came up with certain invoices, went to the police, and that the property was returned to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you did go with Mr. Colak to a village near Knin and you happened to come upon items that Mr. Colak recognised?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Knin, and I met them down there. I asked them for a ride, because I was on foot. I went to Knin on several occasions, just to enjoy myself to go to the fort, and visit some friends who had, by that time, come to Knin, Croatian soldiers who returned to their homes. That's how I met him as well. Even if I had stolen anything, there is nothing that I would have been ashamed of. This was all ours, not theirs. Even if I had been helping them, I would have told you. But I was not helping them, I was merely hitching a ride.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just tell me again from which village was Mr. Colak from. Where did he live before Operation Storm or throughout?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: He's from Piramatovci, as I just said. It is next to my village, the same parish; we had the same church and graveyard. It is one kilometres away from my village, but by now the two have merged. The three Croatian villages in that area are merged, and they gravitate to the same church. The All Saints Church in that parish.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So explain again to me. How did these items this three-seat sofa, the armchair, a double bed, small cabinet, carpet, move from Piramatovci to that village next to Knin during the war? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: What do you mean how? Not just that, everything was taken away. I told you at the beginning of the hearing that they even took the stone from the houses. They took away everything. They looted all Croatian villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go to the next item I want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, some of us would like to have an answer. If you know, tell us how the owner of this three-seat sofa, how he came across that sofa at a distance of some 20 or 25 or 30 kilometres from the place where he used to live? Did he go through all the houses to look whether his sofa was there or ... Could you explain to us what seems to be quite a coincidence that you suddenly recognise at what place your own sofa, and apart from that also an armchair a double bed, if they were found in the same place. Could you explain to us how this happened, whether you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I just met him on the road and asked him to take me to Vodice because that's where I was accommodated as a refugee in the camp there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he tell you that this was his -- his own stuff, or was it that you assumed that this was his own stuff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He told me it was his stuff when we were stopped by the police. He told them that he recognised his own stuff, the closet -- this was a set of furniture that he recognised. He asserted that quite firmly. He was convinced it was his. And I learned it was later on returned to him. As for how he came across that, I don't know whether he was wondering about the area or whether somebody told him. That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you told us is what you heard him tell the police when he was stopped; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the second part of the story, that he still found the invoices, how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I learned that later, much later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was released from prison. He is a distant cousin of mine. When I came to Vodice after the jail, I asked him about the closets and he said, Yes, the police returned it to me. He was an honest, hard-working man. He has a house in Vodice and Piramatovci. The house in Piramatovci was completely looted, and he was probably looking for his stuff. It's not just that the closet was taken away; his livestock, his tractor was taken away, everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He told you that he got it back from the police. Did he tell you or did he ever show you the invoices or is that what you assume; or, if you heard that, from whom did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd have to guess, but I don't want to lie or put anyone into any trouble, either him or myself. I don't remember many details. I don't even remember the names of the soldiers I was with in Operation Storm, and now you're asking me to provide you with details concerning some beds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm quite serious about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you don't remember from whom you heard about these invoices that may have convinced the police to return these items? Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't ask me these, what I believe, are silly things. I can't even recall who I was with in the Storm, let alone who stole what, who had what invoices, what beds, silly stuff like that. That was no theft. We were returning our property. They had nothing. They were poor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I asked you because you testified about it. Mr. Waespi will now proceed. Mr. Waespi, how much time would you still need? Because it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Ten, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten, 15 minutes. That's too much to do before the break. We will first have a break, and then we resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, the last issue which was left over from the previous session, in paragraph 4 of your witness statement, and I have quoted from that already, you said that you: "... remained in the area of Ivosevci and continued to participate in carrying out tasks to the best of my abilities. This continued until I was apprehended." And you were apprehended on the 11th of September, 1995, after the murder of Dara Milosevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's briefly go to the rape of that woman. In relation to the murder, you told us that it was a coincidence. Was the rape of this woman also a coincidence?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: What does that mean, coincidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think you tried to explain the way you killed Dara Milosevic, and you just said, It just happened, you know, it was a coincidence. That's what I picked up, page 11.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was it a coincidence that this woman who was, as you knew, fairly old, that she was raped?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: She was not raped. Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's have 65 ter 7316, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe you told us earlier that you were indeed in the house of the victim - whose name, I suggest, we don't mention, and perhaps we shouldn't broadcast this report, because I frankly don't whether the victim is still alive or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the document will not be broadcasted, and we'll avoid mentioning names. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, this is the criminal report, dated 11 October, 1995, that went to the district public attorney, and it names you in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any objection to go through this. If we're going to go through this in this fashion, then as opposed to just having 65 ter - what is the two numbers, the two documents that I offered at the end as MFI numbers? - and they would be 1 -- D1551 MFI, 1D552 [sic] MFI. Then if we're going to go into this with this fashion, then I would just offer those into evidence because we're -- actually we're talking about the same individual, so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think there are two procedural -- different procedural ways. I'm obviously objecting to credibility of this witness, so it's for a different purpose that I'm tendering the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That could be part, then, of your submissions whether it makes any difference for what purpose. It is for the truth of the content or whether it's about challenging the credibility of the witness. Whether that makes any differences would be part of your submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I mean, I -- if, in fact, he's challenging the credibility of the witness and on that basis he is moving forward, I presented that exact argument yesterday with yesterday's witness to which the Prosecution objected. I frankly don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be MFI. You have ample opportunity to -- well ample opportunity, another 25 words. Now, you're gaining more and more words to explain your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Don't worry, Judge, we don't use them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just -- what I'm saying is that if it's going to be tendered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, do you see yourself as one of the suspects in paragraph 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In the English, it's on page 3, and in Croatian it is on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you see your name there?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to page 5 of the English, and in B/C/S, it's page 3, the lower part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it first talks that the same woman was raped before, a couple of weeks before, by a similar group of people, including Nikola Bilic. Do you know Nikola Bilic?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: A neighbour of mine and a cousin. We're all related in the village, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So he was raping this woman, together with others, a group rape; and a few days later, on the 3rd of September, you joined the group and rape this old woman again. Isn't that what happened?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So this --

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: This is your assertion. She herself told the court that she had not been raped. We were robust, we were drunk, it was 2.00 or 3.00 in the morning, but there was no rape.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you got one year for nothing.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Well, not for nothing. I was charged with an attempt to rape, and for mistreatment. And if there was a rape -- if there were a rape, I would have gotten 80 years of prison. But I was also charged with insulting the person, the way we entered the house, since it was 1.00, 2.00, 3.00 in the morning, we asked for wine. Some people were asking for some oxen. In the end, I fell asleep drunk on the couch. I woke up in the morning. What rape? Don't even mention that. It's an ugly word.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And on the same page in English you see that everybody involved on the 3rd of September was wearing uniforms, military uniforms, and was carrying weapons. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know about the others. I know about myself. We were a group of drunkards doing stupid things without orders of our own accord. We were more or less all drunk. What else can I tell you? I'm a bit confused. We would gather in a bar, have drinks, then someone would say there were some cattle and oxen there, and that was the point of going. As for the old lady, no one raped her. When I entered the house, I did shout, Whore, Chetnik whore, give us something to drink. I told the court that, and I'm not denying that, but that I raped her or that someone beat her, that is not correct. She herself confirmed that in the court. She was belittled, disparaged, humiliated. That's why we were sentenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move on to a last document --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to tender that, marked for identification, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar this document to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2563, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's pull up 65 ter 7317.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bilic, you were not the only member of the 15th Home Guard Regiment arrested in suspicion of having committed serious crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you aware that in October 1995 there was a peaceful protest?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This can be broadcast, Mr. President, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: A peaceful protest held by members of the 15th Home Guard Regiment, and I quote from this document: "Since several demobilized members of their unit have been the subject of criminal investigation and have been arrested on reasonable grounds for suspicion that they have committed the crime of murder." Were I aware of this advance of solidarity from the other members of the 15th Home Guard Regiment to their colleagues who were demobilised?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2564.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bilic, you told us that your sentence was reduced by, I think twice, first by the president, President Tudjman, and the second on the day of the Croatian national holiday. What day was that, the Croatian national holiday?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: The 13th of May, but it was changed in 2001, when there was a change in government. I don't know what it was called. I don't know what the new date is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us again why, on a Croatian national holiday, you were -- your sentence was reduced, a sentence you had served for murder?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Why it was reduced? Why wouldn't it? I was ill, I behaved well, and I was about to undergo an operation. I had bullet wounds and -- although I may appear rather healthy. I was sick, and I sent an application for pardon, and President Tudjman pardoned me. The same happened on another occasion, because I behaved well in the prison, and I was ill. I spent more time in the military hospital in Pula, than in the jail itself. I was under treatment non-stop. I have papers to show -- to prove that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I omitted to tender 1D987; that's the military police report of 14 September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the one which was not shown. Is that all --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, that's a previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the previous one. Then we're now talking about the one which is still on our screen. It's about the protest. Mr. Registrar, am I mistaken that -- I think we -- it was tendered. It was even admitted, or am I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the document -- the last document was MFI'd -- will be MFI'd under seal for the same purposes for which it was not shown to the public. And then, Mr. Registrar, could you please repeat the identity of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was 65 ter number 1D987, and that will become Exhibit P2565.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Gwaunza has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Yes, I want to ask you a question concerning the case that you mentioned in which you were convicted and sentenced one year and which is right now on appeal. Would have you any idea why it took so long for the case to go to trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer. It was not heard by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe some of them were not within reach. How should I know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have few questions for you. You told us that when you were in Ivosevci that you were guarding -- I think the water tank and the church or two churches, as you said, in or near Kistanje. Now, who had selected these objects to be guarded?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I was the first one to enter Kistanje, so I was the one to decide that first. I assigned two lads to stand guard by the church so that it not be demolished, and that's something that the first news coverage from Knin covered. The TV crew filmed the area, and you could see that not a single house was damaged while I was there, all the way to Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have referred to this television recording several times. Do you still possess a copy? Or have any of the parties have a copy? Do you still have a copy with you which shows your interview on the television?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: The television would have it; I don't. I never asked to be given a copy. But they must have it for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. You said that you captured several men and that you handed them over. Now, what was the distance you had to take them in order to hand them over? I think it was in Bribirske Most, or am I mistaken? At what distance is that?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: The police would come. We didn't have to go a long way. The military police would come. Initially there was a wounded individual and we called the Medical Corps who were located close to us, and they came within 20 minutes. As far as those captured are concerned, the military police would come and take them over to, I guess, the prison facilities in Zadar, or, rather, Sibenik, Split, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, when you were performing your tasks, if I could say so, your self-assigned tasks, when you were in the area of -- the area of Ivosevci, where did you stay at night?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: During the night, for a while, we spent nights in Ivosevci for the first several days before my leg started giving me trouble and I had to go to Vodice. When we were capturing Chetniks, we would spent nights up there, or, rather, we would not be sleeping. Let me illustrate this. There were some ten of us, five or six would be singing Ustasha songs and then we would pretend to be leaving the village while, in actual fact, four of five of us would stay behind. And that's how we managed to capture the Chetniks. They would not surrender. This was ten or 20 days following Operation Storm, and they kept hiding in the woods in the area which had very tall trees sticking at least two metres above our heads, and we knew ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was ask about where you stayed at night, and I do understand that you still were on duty, to some extent, during the evening and night hours as well. You said you stayed for a couple of days in -- stayed for a couple of days in -- in Ivosevci, and then you returned to Vodice. Now, after you had returned to Vodice, where you had lived for a while, if I understand you well, did you then return to the Kistanje area later?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Of course, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How did you travel from Ivosevci to Vodice?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: There was always some sort of military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that a vehicle belonging to the unit you had been a member of or was it just one that would pass?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: For the most part, we would hitch a ride from the vehicles passing by. You see, I had to go to the emergency ward in Vodice on several occasions to have water taken out of my knee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you use your own transportation? Did you have a car?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I had, but I did not use it in the early days. It was only later on when we were binge drinking and overeating and in all that madness, where the story of that old woman came in and this was without anyone's consent, approval, or without anyone's order, something that we did of our own accord, on own initiative, several of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was about your car, nothing else. That car, was it your car when you were arrested in September - I think it was September - that was seized by the police?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was not my car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whose car was that?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I can't even remember at this stage. We picked it up somewhere, or it may have belonged to someone; I don't remember. It was not mine. I had my own car, at the time it was Golf 1, and I used it at a later stage, when we went binge drinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said this car you might have picked it up somewhere. Just to say was it for you a car which may have belonged to someone else and you took it?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I can't tell you. I may have borrowed it. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to understand that you don't remember whether it was a car you borrowed, which I understand to be borrowing from someone you know, or a car which belongs to someone you do not know. Which of the two was it? If you could tell us.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Truly, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you exclude for the possibility that it was a car which was stolen?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I do not. However, I suppose that they took all their valuables with them, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say, there was no car left to be stolen because everyone would have taken his car. Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now a different matter. You've told us that the police couldn't do anything about looting. At the same time, you tell us that a car was stopped with quite a number of household items on it. Could you tell us where that happened?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You got a ride from someone who had apparently a red three-seat couch, an armchair, and some other household goods loaded, and you were stopped by the police. Could you tell us where that happened?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: As I said before, I met the man somewhere along the road, I don't know precisely where, and he gave me a lift home to Vodice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And where was the police that stopped this car?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that either. There were quite a few check-points. I simply can't remember. There was one at Bribirske Mostine, there was one at Cista Mala, there was one close to Vodice, manned by both the military and civilian police. This was a vast territory, and some check-points could be avoided. The police could simply not cover the entire territory. It was so vast that not even a higher number of policemen could cover it. If I wanted to take away anything, I could have, because we were familiar with every inch of the territory, with every bush. The police could not stop us and prevent us from doing what we intended to do if we really applied ourselves to it. As far as the army is concerned, everything went fine as far as Ivosevci. From then on, I'll be frank, we were doing things our own way. And I'm not talking about units, I'm talking about individuals.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat what he said mentioning generals.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: This is the truth, and I'm telling you the way things were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you told us about --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, there is an interlineation from the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then let me just ... In your -- you said "from then," and I think you were talking about from --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think he mentioned as far as Ivosevci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Ivosevci is concerned. "From then ..." you said, and you would be frank, you "... were doing things our own way. And I'm not talking about units, I'm talking about individuals." Now, did you say anything in relation to generals there? The interpreters ask us whether you said anything about generals.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said the following, and this is what I think, and I'm telling you frankly. All the misdeeds, alleged misdeeds, if they were indeed done there is a still a question mark, I should be the first one to be sitting here in the dock as long as -- alongside everybody else who did these crimes. From Ivosevci onwards, it was us individuals who committed these ill-deeds. Let's call them that way. These are innocent people who you captured here along with families and entire Croatia. It is criminals and murders such as I am who should be sitting here, and I do stand by what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, as far as these check-points are concerned, you told us about -- for example, about tractors being transported. How would you pass a check-point with a tractor?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I've already said that had there been a 1001 check-points and had there been twice as many policemen as there were those of us, we would still find passages to pass them by. The police manned check-points, and we knew every single forest trail and path which would enable us to circumvent the police and go around these check-points. I'm telling you this because I myself did that on several occasions, and I was carrying a lamb or a piece of ham, and I managed to get around the police. Had I gone passed where the police was, they would have confiscated those things off me. One could pass freely if one wanted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, this Chamber has heard evidence - I'm not referring to all of the evidence but some evidence - also indicating that sometimes at check-points, goods that might have been stolen, that those manning the check-points were not very sharp on seizing those objects. Did it ever happen to you that you passed a check-point where you were not bothered that much about what you were transporting?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: That's not true. The police did their job properly and seized items. Once the military caught me and took they the wine that I had and ham, but I saw at Bribirske Mostine at the check-point there dozens of tractors that the police had taken from people who engaged in thieving or let's call it looting. They claimed that they belonged to them but they couldn't prove it. So the police would seize the items from them, and subsequently if they had documentation proving that they were owners of tractors or anything else, the police would return them. Of course, it was only few people who had any documentation to present, since they had been expelled from their homes barefoot with a plastic bag in their hands. I can tell you what happened on the first day when the Chetniks barged in our village, a hundred or 200 people were gathered by them, herded together, and then they were shot at, their feet were shot at. They had to run from Hrkovici to Raslina across ragged terrain, not along paths. In Raslina by the lake, they were received by still other people who transported them across the lake to Bilice where they spent -- my parents and my entire village spent one month in exile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One final question: When you were in Ivosevci, you were asked about under whose command you were at that time. I think you said that you didn't know who, exactly, your commander was, if I understood you well. Could you tell us what his rank was?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know. I had not been fighting with them before. They had their own battalion. There was one battalion in Vodice, another one in Skradin, and a third was stationed, I can't remember where. I can't recall it at this time. At any rate, this was a large stretch. Our battalion, the 5th Regiment covered the area from Stankovci, all the way to Sibenik. It was a large swathe. I don't know where one of the battalions was stationed. I was in the intervention platoon in Vodice, which was part of the regiment. We were stationed at the so-called sugar factory. There was one platoon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When was that exactly?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: -- and we were engaged in interventions actions. Right from the start. Perhaps a month or two after the inception of the regiment that a intervention platoon led by Colonel Krunoslav Lazarin [phoen] was set up. Although I had undergone training earlier on at Mala Luka, we subsequently attended training in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you when this happened in relation to the start of Operation Storm. You're talking about the battalion structure. I was asking you about the time you spent in - and I'm -- I'm again having difficulties in finding the right name. When you were doing your own tasks, after you -- you stood, you were guarding the water tower, you were guarding the churches, you stayed in Ivosevci. Are you talking about this period in time? Because I was asking about your command, your commander, at the time when you were in Ivosevci.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know his name. I didn't see him. The command was stationed in Skradin, so I didn't know who they were. I only came to know the name later on when I had to reconstruct my war path. His name was Selimir Vuksic or something like that. I don't know him personally. He was in Skradin, and I was in the lower battlefield of Vodice, some ten kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Kinis has a question in relation to this matter, apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that you -- you were received the task to provide some search of abandoned houses in Kistanje and you also mentioned during your testimonies that you find a lot of weapons here. Did you receive, prior this operation, some -- some instructions how to deal with these weapons which you will find in these abandoned houses? Whether there was some rules which -- which says that you should submit some reports of outcome of this operations or you just deal with these weapons by yourself and keep at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: As far as the orders are concerned about the code of conduct, that's something that the Croatian army received back in 1992, 1993, including the brigades and regiments. We were all familiar with the code of military conduct prior to the operation. Now, going back to the weapons, the weapons found in Kistanje and in these villages, we weren't able to carry those weapons along. You could carry not more than three rifles. So we didn't real take the weapons along. The lads who were following in our path were the ones who collected the weapons. I couldn't carry the excess weapons since I had to proceed with the action. Later on, rifles could be found in every house. And at that rate, rifles were handed over to the closest check-points, to the commanders who were there. Since I wasn't a commander, there is nothing more that I can tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: And the next question is: You mentioned that your place where your unit was dispatched was Ivosevci, and from Vodice it is approximately -- no, I'm roughly, will say, 76 to -- 76 or 77 kilometres. Did you ask the permission to somebody to travel to Vodice? Did you have task to return back the next morning for continuing your job? How -- how this command and control chain was working at that time? Because you were a member of army.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. I reached Kistanje. We went on foot. We were walking for a day or two. My foot was swollen, and I asked some lads from the Medical Corps to transport me to the emergency ward, because we had physicians in the basement of the Olimp [phoen] hotel in Vodice. They were there at the ready. So they would take me down there to have my knee emptied of water and then would take me home -- then they take me back. I couldn't go home. I wanted to go back despite my leg, and I was ill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: But who gave you permission for you to do so? And also you mentioned that you were on your own in the shed of, for instance, three nights; you were hiding at this victim's house and waiting for this person who -- who you wanted to -- at that time arrest. Who -- who did some control over you, over behaviour of -- of soldiers at that time? You said you don't know who is your superior, you don't know who is your platoon commander and so, but -- but who -- was there actually some kind of control over behaviour of soldiers or soldiers were freely to move during the night, whatever they want?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: No. You mentioned the murder and all that, but that took place later. At first, everything was known who did what where and when and who can do what things. We knew what the orders were. Later on, as of Ivosevci onwards, which was a few days after Operation Storm, the guys who could, went further afield. Some stayed behind, guarding the towers, churches, et cetera. I joined them. I don't know who they belonged to, what platoons or what; but I could enter any squad or join any platoon because everyone knew me. We all knew each other down there. This was no American army. We were just plain soldiers; farmers become soldiers overnight. Some things we did independently. Without orders, without any order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the questions by the Bench raised any need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, first I would like to show you D204, which is an order of General Gotovina dated 10 August 1995. Mr. Bilic, this is an order by General Gotovina on compliance with military disciplinary measures. Now, you were asked questioned by Mr. Waespi concerning your activities and just Judge Kinis concerning some movement, and I turn to number 1 in this order. It says: "I prohibit arbitrary movement of HV members in the liberated areas without the knowledge of ... superior commanders." And number 2: "Take all necessary measures and fully engage in the implementation of the military disciplinary conduct and maintenance of order in the area of responsibility and prevent arson and all other illegal acts." Now, the question Mr. Waespi asked you about, if you received an order from General Gotovina, would you follow it, did you receive this order from General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, obviously that doesn't arise from my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Of course, it does. Of course, it does. You just asked the question in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to get -- let's focus on the matter. Have you seen this order ever before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Personally, no. I was not a commander. But I do know that it was stressed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question simply was whether the answer is "no." Were you ever given an order that arbitrary movement of HV members in the liberated areas without knowledge of the superior commanders was prohibited? So that HV soldiers could not arbitrarily move around without knowledge of their commanders. Did you ever receive such an order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course we did. In the course of the first few days we couldn't even go anywhere. We were told not to mingle because we were all assigned our own insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's talk about well, let's say, let's forget about the first four days, five days, of Operation Storm. After that date, did you ever receive any order which prohibited arbitrary movement of members of the HV in the liberated areas without knowledge of their superior commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I took over some responsibilities of my own initiative, as I already said. Therefore, I blame myself for many things I missed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wasn't asking whether you blame yourself for anything. My question simply was whether you received, after the first four or five days of Operation Storm, whether you -- an order was given to you by whomever. You may tell us who it was, if you received such an order, that arbitrary movement of HV members was not -- was prohibited without knowledge of their superior commanders. Did you ever receive such an order at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. I simply cannot recall. I may have, I may not. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you, at that time -- point in time, did you receive any order - so, again, after this first four or five days - to take all necessary measures to fully engage in the implementation of military disciplinary conduct? Did you receive such an order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. Maybe I did, maybe I did not. I don't remember such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. A few issues. If I could turn --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could turn to -- and I'm going to cover some issues that were addressed by counsel. The first I'd like to talk about is P2564, and if I could turn to the transcript at page 75, line 21, and this was the last document counsel showed you concerning this rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you were asked in -- on line 21 by Mr. Waespi: "Were you aware that in October 1995 there was a peaceful protest?" If I can scroll up here. And let me read the bottom part of this document that wasn't read going over to the next page and this is coming from General Lausic. "We are herewith forwarding to the the above said intelligence report for your information and an order for you to take adequate measures to prevent the potential protest rally from taking place." Now, that wasn't read to you. And I believe, if we scroll down, your answer, if I can, is that you don't recall any such rally.

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: By that time I was already in jail, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you were in jail at this point. That's fine, sir. Let's turn our attention, I want to cover another item. And that is P2565 when counsel talked to you. That is a two-page document, if we can. So five pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this the one not to be shown on the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do not -- no, no it's not. It has to do with the stop on the 23rd of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your testimony, both on cross-examination and some questions asked by the Bench, you have talked about check-points and this the check-point you were stopped as you approached Vodice and you were driving a Lada vehicle. Now is that Lada vehicle a military vehicle or a civilian vehicle?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, and with regard to these seizures -- well, let's just take that one step further. I mean, this was a Lada with no number plates. Now, military vehicles have an HV-numbered plate on it, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is leading. This is leading, and the witness answered already, that he doesn't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking him a question based on his knowledge of HV vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do HV military vehicles have a licence plate with an HV designation and a number?

utterances.speaker: VESELKO BILIC
utterances.text: Yes they had their own plates. I believe they were yellow, HV plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
